Question: As a computer engineer what coding languages should I learn (name them please)?
Answer: Don’t worry about which languages matter when you are starting out. Instead, think of it this way: through your career you will more than likely use lots of languages. I’ve lost count. I know it’s more than 40, though the vast majority of my work has been in only six of those. So the trick is to learn how to learn languages quickly. You do this by learning lots of languages early on. But first, you have to learn programming, which is a language-independent skill. Unfortunately, you have to learn a whole stack of things simultaneously when you start out: programming itself, debugging, some language, and some set of tools that will let you use that language (an editor, maybe a build system, maybe a debugger, version control…) Your first language should probably be something relatively easy, as you have all that extra load to deal with. Easy languages, however, are not typically the really important languages, either important because they’re widely used in industry, or important because of what they teach you. Later, whatever your first language, you should spend a bit of time learning one from each major language family (procedural, functional, object oriented, dynamic, lazily evaluated, declarative, etc). That will make the ones you have to learn later much easier.

Question: Can a transport layer protocol be created that has better performance than TCP and UDP?
Answer: Sure. You do have to define ‘performance’ and ‘better’, though, because there are multiple possible definitions and the differences matter. QUIC (as used in HTTP/3) may be the leading contender for that better protocol. But SCTP, DTLS, LEDBAT, and a few others, might also be better, depending on what exactly you want. If you are working in this field, you also need to be aware that QUIC, TCP, and SCTP are all moving targets; they get frequent upgrades too. So what it means to be “better than TCP” may not remain the same from month to month.

Question: Do multiple people sharing an Internet connection each have their own unique external IP address?
Answer: Most of the time, in IPv4, no. Almost always in IPv6, yes. IPv4 does not have enough addresses to number the current Internet, so addresses are shared, by use of NAT (network address translation, which comes in several varieties). In fact, it’s fairly common that external IP addresses will be shared between multiple connections (so-called Carrier Grade NAT, for example). More than likely you have never used a network that didn’t share IPv4 addresses. IPv6 has plenty of addresses, so while NAT is possible, it’s very rare. Most devices on an IPv6 network will have many addresses, in fact. So… it depends.

Question: Is there a belief that Go language will eventually replace Java and C++? Are there any perceived advantages of Go language over these languages?
Answer: No. Originally the designers of Go had replacing C (not C++) in mind. But as the language developed, it has turned out to be more suitable as a replacement for Python. Go is a pretty decent language, but it turns out to be best for small to medium sized or loosely coupled applications, much like Python. It’s also not really suitable for kernel-like situations, so it can’t replace C there. There are a lot of system management and monitoring utilities written in Go (Prometheus, many parts of Kubernetes), and development of new applications of that sort in Python has basically stopped.

Question: Why don't aircraft use the jet stream in the atmosphere to fly faster or save energy?
Answer: Before you ask why not, ask if. They do, any time it’s possible. There are companies that specialise in constructing flight plans that make the absolute most of the current weather situation, using jet streams and whatever else might be going on. Airlines pay them for those flight plans when they need to get a flight somewhere in the minimum possible time. Some airlines do a lot of that work in-house, especially those that have many intercontinental routes (because obviously, the longer the flight, the more difference this makes). There are even some routes that are only possible because each flight has a team of people at the airline continuously working on weather optimisation, and communicating the results to the flight crew in real time.

Question: Is it possible to use aluminum instead of wood for making guitars and other stringed instruments? Would it be a suitable material for the body parts such as the neck and bridge?
Answer: Yes, it’s possible. For some parts, like electric guitar bridges, it’s completely normal to use aluminium. Others, like tuners, it’s not quite normal but still common. Aluminium is also a common ingredient in a bronze alloy used for some acoustic guitar strings. People have used aluminium for necks, fretboards, and even pretty much the whole instrument. It’s not actually a great material for neck and fretboard, because while it sounds fine and looks cool, it also feels too cold to play comfortably. I played an aluminium neck bass once, it sounded great but gave me cramp very quickly because the room was pretty cold. Double bass players will be familiar with this issue because the strings themselves are enough of a heat sink to be a problem. Aluminium frets are a bad idea, it’s too soft and will wear out quickly. Composites like carbon fiber and Richlite are usually preferable if you’re looking for non-wood alternatives for structural parts. Plastics are possible, 3D printed guitar bodies are quite doable. Nevertheless… this is a real instrument: Note the wood neck.

Question: Is it possible for pilots to recover from spins? Is practicing spin recovery part of their flight training or just a theoretical concept taught in the curriculum?
Answer: Some airplanes can recover from spins, some can not. Some are almost impossible to spin in the first place. Pilots can recover any recoverable airplane, and the recovery procedure is part of the type rating. In some cases the recovery procedure is as simple as “release the controls, throttle back, and wait”. Or it may require placing the controls in a specific position (centered and all the way forward is common). However, not every country requires actual spin training as part of the license process. Many common training airplanes are in the “almost impossible to spin” category. Nearly all large airplanes are in the “can not recover” category. So flying schools would most likely have to specifically buy an aerobatic airplane for the purpose of spin training, which is rather onerous. Training always does cover incipient spins and how to recognise that the next thing that happens would be a spin, and how to recover before the spin becomes fully developed. Nearly all airplanes can recover from an incipient spin, and the exceptions are all very unusual military types.

Question: Is it possible to tune an electric guitar to the same strings as an acoustic guitar? Are they essentially the same instrument?

Question: What causes the wings to stall before the tail of an airplane?
Answer: Deliberate design. Planes are designed so that the horizontal tail will stall at an angle of attack greater than that required to stall the wing. Usually that’s only for an upright stall, though for aerobatic aircraft and fighters they typically require this for inverted stalls as well. Why? Turns out it’s hard to recognise that you’ve stalled the tail, and relatively easy to recognise that the wing is stalled. So it’s safer. Also, some takeoff and landing techniques are more useful if you can easily and reliably fully stall the wing during the process.

Question: Can you take off without flaps on an airplane? If so, how long will it fly before it crashes due to lack of lift?
Answer: In small planes, if you have a long enough runway, you can safely take off, fly around, and land again without a problem. You do have to take off much faster than you would with the flaps, which is why you need more runway. Really big aircraft, including many airliners and military transports, don’t have tyres which would survive going that fast on the ground, nor would their landing gear stay intact at that speed. But in principle, if runways were long enough and airplane wheels strong enough, no particular problem. Trying to take off at a speed calculated for a certain amount of flap extension without those flaps actually extended, though, is a really serious mistake, and will probably lead to a crash one way or another.

Question: Is it possible for people to connect to your home wifi if they are in range, even if your network is hidden from view on the router?

Question: Is it possible for an airplane to land without its nose wheel touching down first? If so, what would happen and would it be due to aerodynamics and physics?
Answer: Correct landing technique for a tricycle airplane is to touch down main gear first, and nose wheel only later. If you don’t, you’re risking a ground loop (basically, in car terms, you spin out and crash). The reason you can do this is that you are flying very slowly, which requires a high angle of attack, which requires a nose-high attitude. This also means that there is a maximum speed at which you can safely touch down, because the angle of attack would be too low and the nose wheel would touch first.

Question: When HTTP is used over TCP, which happens first, HTTP’s GET request or TCP’s 3-way handshake?
Answer: It depends. If it’s HTTP/3, there isn’t going to be a TCP handshake, and the GET request can be carried in the QUIC handshake along with everything else. If you have a fast reconnect token, the handshake doesn’t happen, you just get a resumed session with an immediate response. If it’s HTTP/2 or below, and you have a valid TCP fast reconnect token, there isn’t going to be a TCP handshake, and the GET request is in the first packet. If it’s HTTP/2 or below and you have an invalid token or no token at all, the GET request comes after the handshake; if the token was invalid, the request will likely have to be retransmitted.

Question: Can using heavier or lighter strings on an electric guitar affect its tuning? If so, to what extent? Is there a way to prevent this from happening?
Answer: Yes, it will. Well, not tuning, but intonation. The difference is this: tuning is the pitches to which you adjust the open strings. That you can get correct easily with any reasonable string. But intonation is the pitch at each fret. Even if the open string is in tune, that does not mean all the frets are. When the instrument was set up, it was intonated to a particular set of strings. If you change them to another set of the exact same type, there should be minimal effect on the intonation. If, however, you change gauges, or change to a material with a different density, then the change in tension as you fret notes will be different, and the intonation will be off. In other words, the open strings can be right, but the further up the fretboard you go, the worse the tuning gets. This can be fixed by redoing the intonation parts of the setup… adjusting the bridge saddle positions, heights, and maybe the truss rod, so that the pitches line up with the frets again. If you have a tremelo, that will need adjusted too (which takes a lot of work… this isn’t easy and won’t be cheap). Either learn how to do this properly, which is way too much to describe in a Quora answer, or decide on what strings you want to use, then take the instrument to a setup technician or luthier and get them to get it right… then keep using exactly the same kind of strings.

Question: Are business class seats really that much more comfortable than economy?

Question: Can you provide an explanation for why time slows down near objects with strong gravitational fields, like neutron stars or black holes, but not near planets or the Sun which have weaker gravitational fields in comparison?
Answer: Time does slow down near smaller objects too… just much less. So, for example, it shows up in the orbit of Mercury as a tiny change in the shape of the orbit due to gravitational time dilation from the Sun. A dedicated amateur astronomer could do the work to demonstrate that, over a period of a year or two, with reasonably priced equipment. It shows up due to gravitational time dilation from the Earth too, if you have good enough equipment to detect it. That’s within the budget of a (moderately wealthy) amateur scientist. I could do it if I wanted, with my own money. State of the art timing equipment can detect the gravitational time dilation due to the mass of a moderate sized mountain. I could do that too, though I couldn’t pay for it.

Question: What company makes an electric bass guitar that has only one bolt holding the neck on? I've tried Googling it (images and all), but every guitar they show with a bolted on neck has four bolts?
Answer: There’s a straightforward structural reason for that. The neck needs to be constrained sufficiently to stay properly positioned, and clamped in to place. Bolt-on necks are primarily there to simplify the joinery of the neck-body interface, to make the instrument both cheaper and more robust. One bolt could be sufficient clamping force to retain a bass neck, but to constrain the neck such that it would not rotate around that bolt would require precision joinery around the neck pocket. That rather defeats the purpose of using a bolt-on at all. Three is the minimum possible to constrain the position and all rotations, but the trouble with that is that you also want the bolts to be quite short, and that limits the clamping force you can generate. So most bolt-ons have at least four bolts, sometimes as many as six.

Question: What are the differences between gasoline and jet fuel? Can they be used interchangeably?
Answer: No, they can not be used interchangeably. Jet fuel is high-quality kerosene. You can run it in many diesel engines, if you’re careful about fuel pump lubrication, but a gasoline engine won’t like it at all. You can also use it to run any kerosene-fired heater or other appliance. Aviation gasoline is high-octane leaded gasoline, and will work in any gasoline engine that will tolerate the lead (most road vehicle engines built in the last 40 years will not).

Question: What are the rules for bringing prescription medication on an airplane? What are the consequences if law enforcement finds it during a pat down or search?
Answer: Domestic flights in every country I’m aware of: No problem, just follow the liquids rules if any of it is liquid, though there are exceptions for medicines. Look them up. International travel: Make sure your essential prescriptions are legal in all the countries you will be passing through before you buy the tickets. Make sure you have documentation that the medicine was actually prescribed (many countries have pharmacies put stickers on the packaging, so don’t repack your medicines unless you have copies of the actual prescriptions). Obviously, consider if the prescription is essential if it’s not legal where you are going. The common issues are Marijuana derivatives in many countries, Modafinil and ADHD medications going to Japan. Look up and understand the rules for the particular country. Often it is legal for a visitor to bring in and use prescriptions that would be illegal to prescribe in that country. But remember: prescription medications are a specific category in air transport and customs regulations all over the world, and are mostly allowed. You just have to show that yes, they really are prescription, and make sure to respect the exceptions.

Question: The EV was invented before the gas car. The gas car killed off the EV market by the free market. Why do some people think all people will switch to EV this time?
Answer: In the meantime, we have invented three crucial technologies that make all the difference. One, better batteries. All they had then was lead-acid, which… well, are made of lead. They’re really heavy for their energy capacity. Modern batteries are vastly better. Two, MOSFETs. All they had was manual switches (which means no throttle control) or resistive control (meaning really horrible efficiency). MOSFETs enable switch-mode electronic speed control, which gives an efficiency around 90% and perfect throttle control. MOSFETs also allow much more efficient and faster chargers. Three, microcontrollers. These allow us to control those MOSFETs accurately, and keep track of the battery charge. Without those, you had no way to know how much range remained in your batteries, other than the performance starting to drop. This is, admittedly, much worse with modern batteries, which tend to perform pretty much the same till the charge gets really low and then suddenly die.

Question: Is it possible to land without glide slope in real life aviation, or is it only achievable in flight simulators?
Answer: Yes, and every pilot knows how. What isn’t possible is doing that when you can’t see the runway. One way or another you need precision vertical guidance, and there’s only three ways to do that: visual, ILS, or GPS. The latter two use the glide slope, and work in poor visibility. Visual landings without glide slope are entirely normal, and very common.
